chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Zurara and Harun ibn Muslim from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said) who said:

He asked me, 'Does Ibn Abi Layla rule with a legal judgment and then return from it?' I said to him, 'It has reached me that he ruled regarding the property of a man and a woman when one of them dies, and the heirs of the living and the heirs of the deceased claim it, or the man divorces her, and the man claims it and the woman claims it, in four different rulings.' He said, 'And what are they?' I said, 'As for the first of that, he ruled in it according to the saying of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i - he would make the property of the woman that which is not for the man belong to the woman, and the property of the men that which is not for the women belong to the man, and what is for both men and women, they split it in half. Then it reached me that he said,

I said to him, 'The property becomes for the woman.' He said, 'What do you see if she presents evidence, to how many does she need?' I said, 'Two witnesses.' He said, 'If you asked from between her two thighs, meaning the two mountains, and we were at that time in Mecca, they would inform you that the dowry and property are openly given from the house of the woman to the house of her husband, so she is the one who brought it, and he is the claimant. If he claims that he created something in it, let him bring evidence upon it.'

key_terms.إِبْرَاهِيمُ النَّخَعِيُّ: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, a famous early jurist whose opinions were cited
key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي لَيْلَى: Ibn Abi Layla, a prominent early Islamic judge
key_terms.مَتَاع: Property, goods, or movable assets (specifically marital property here)

ai.seo_question: How did the judge Ibn Abi Layla rule on the division of marital property according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates Ibn Abi Layla’s final ruling on marital property (matāʿ), confirming that the husband retains ownership of the household while the wife keeps her specific belongings, with the burden of proof for new additions resting on the husband. This narration highlights the scholarly practice of accepting a judge's final position even if he reverted to an earlier opinion, emphasizing the principle that marital goods are typically brought by the wife from her family home unless proven otherwise.
